text:
Organic chemists routinely check reaction mixtures and purifications by TLC or column chromatography.  
On a TLC plate each component travels upward; well-separated compounds give distinct spots.  
When two substances have very similar polarities they travel the same distance, giving a single spot (or two spots “right on top of each other”).  The chemist’s complaint that “my compounds are on top of each other” therefore almost certainly means the spots (or bands) in the chromatographic separation are coincident because the compounds have nearly the same polarity.

(A) Similar boiling points would be a distillation problem; the usual phrasing would be “they co-distill,” not that they’re “on top of each other.”  
(B) Similar optical rotations says nothing about separation.  
(C) Non-covalent association could broaden peaks but wouldn’t be described this way.

Thus the most plausible interpretation is:

Answer: D
